newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Zairean rebel chief holds S.African talks -diplomat.
newsitem.headline: Zairean rebel chief holds S.African talks -diplomat.

text.p: Zairean rebel leader Laurent Kabila has held talks with South African officials who hope to broker a ceasefire in the central African country, diplomats told South African radio on Wednesday.
State radio quoted one diplomat, who did not want to be named, as saying Kabila met deputy foreign minister Aziz Pahad in Pretoria on Tuesday after flying into South Africa.
The secretive talks, also attended by U.N. special envoy Mohamed Sahnoun, were due to continue on Wednesday, he said.

Officials from South Africa, Zaire and the United States, whose assistant secretary of state for African affairs, George Moose, is in South Africa to help facilitate the talks, refuse to comment or even to acknowledge that Kabila is in the country.
But one South African source told Reuters they hoped to have some progress to report by Thursday at the latest. A Western diplomat said a swift ceasefire was the main goal of the talks.
Kabila's rebels, many of them Zairean Tutsis whose ethnic kin control neighbouring Rwanda and Burundi, took up arms last October and have overrun a swathe of east Zaire's borderlands.

The conflict, which escalated this month with the aerial bombing of rebel-held towns, has sent tens of thousands of refugees fleeing and threatens to destabilise vast Zaire and its central African neighbours.

President Nelson Mandela, ditching earlier reluctance to get embroiled in efforts to ease the crisis in Africa's Great Lakes region -- Zaire, Rwanda, Burundi and Uganda -- said last week he would host Kabila and Zairean government officials for talks.

Zairean President Mobutu Sese Seko sent his nephew Ngbanda Nzambo Ko Ayumba to South Africa, and rebel representatives met Deputy President Thabo Mbeki last week, but there has been no sign that first face-to-face talks have taken place.
Mandela said he and other African leaders would meet Mobutu on March 19.
Rebel sources said Kabila would not see Mobutu's officials in South Africa, but spokesman Raphael Nghenda said they were happy in principle to talk to the government.
"We are the ones who are in a position of force and we are still in favour of negotiations," he said.

Mobutu's government has so far refused even to recognise the rebels, which is one of the stumbling blocks for the South Africans as they try to bring the two sides together, and has called for a regional summit on the crisis.
Zaire, which accuses Burundi, Rwanda and Uganda of fighting with the rebels, says it will not talk until all foreign troops have left its soil. Its neighbours deny involvement.
South African sources said they wanted to improve on U.N. and other mooted peace plans to find a set of proposals the two warring sides can accept as a starting point for direct talks.

The U.N. plan, adopted last week by the Security Council, calls for an immediate ceasefire, the withdrawal of all foreign forces from Zaire including mercenaries hired by the government, and for Zaire's sovereignty and territory to be respected.
Kabila's forces have met little apparent resistance from Mobutu's ill-disciplined and often unpaid army as they move westwards from their strongholds of Goma and Bukavu.
The rebels, who want to topple Mobutu, say they are only 30 km (18 miles) from the important eastern town of Kindu, where aid workers said residents were in panic.
